Fig. 6 shows the ratio of total measured energy to nominal energy versus the discharge time, at room temperature. The available
energy clearly declines with a shorter discharge time for all types
of battery cells, which means that the available energy is a function of the discharge time (i.e., current rate). Two Li-ion battery
cells (A and B cells) showed a significant voltage drop for short
discharge times (less than 400 s) and their results are not plotted
in Fig. 6. The D cells had the most favorable characteristic from
the viewpoint of available energy with respect to time. Thus, the
D cell was chosen for further analysis. To account for the effects
of discharge time on available energy, energy efficiency ( _ηE_ ) is introduced, and is assumed to be a logarithmic function of discharge
time ( _td_ ). Using the test data in Fig. 6, the energy efficiency of the
D cell is given below.

the mass flow rate of gaseous oxygen leaks from the LOX pump
is assumed to be 0.5% of the nominal flow rate. The bulk temperature and pressure in the cooling channels are also assumed to
be 150 K and 0.2 MPaA, respectively (an average value of leaked
gaseous oxygen from the LOX pump). The electromagnetic loss is
set to be 1.5% of the motor power [29,35]. Fig. 5 shows the predicted rotor temperature according to thrust levels up to 100 kN.
Clearly, the rotor temperatures are under the limit of 403 K and
the use of a PMSM for the ElecPump cycle is valid up to the maximum thrust level of interest in this study. The gaseous mass flow
rates for motor cooling are neglected in this study because they
comprise a relatively small amount of the LOX pump flow rate.

system (internal circuit and software), wires, and a case. Of all the

energy densities is desirable because this ensures a lighter battery
pack. The actual battery cell characteristics are greatly influenced
by the conditions of use. Therefore, a battery cell screening test
